findings.paper_title: Enc. 1 for Budget Monitoring Report to 30 June 2026
findings.headline: Nine staff vacancies as at 30 June 2026, including two key roles not currently advertised
findings.detail: Vacant posts comprise three Loaders, and one each of Grounds Maintenance Operative, HGV Driver, Transport & Parking Officer, Land and Property Information Manager (covered by interim), Planning Officer, and Head of Waste and Environment. The Planning Officer and Head of Waste and Environment posts are not currently advertised. The Council notes that vacancies present 'a major risk of non-delivery of service' where recruitment of suitable candidates is difficult.
findings.matters: Unfilled posts in senior or specialist areas threaten service delivery and income generation (planning fees depend on planning capacity); finance directors track whether budgeted posts will deliver.
findings.figures: 9 vacant posts in General Public Services & Community Engagement; 2 of these not currently advertised
findings.quote: A major risk of non -delivery of service is where key staff leave the Council's employ and there is a delay or difficulty in recruiting suitable candidates to fill the vacant post.

findings.paper_title: Enc. 1 for Budget Monitoring Report to 30 June 2026
findings.headline: Revenue budget shows unfavourable variance of £178,000 (2.7% of budget) at Period 3
findings.detail: The Committee's latest forecast is £6.721m expenditure against a budget of £6.543m. The overspend is concentrated in Housing services (£170,000 of the £178,000 total), with smaller overspends in Community Partnerships (£3,000) and Public Services (£5,000). This is reported in the first quarter of the financial year.
findings.matters: Finance directors must identify whether budget assumptions are holding; peers track spending discipline in comparable services; lenders monitor whether councils maintain expenditure control.

findings.paper_title: Enc. 1 for Budget Monitoring Report to 30 June 2026
findings.headline: Homelessness temporary accommodation requires additional £120,000 budget across 2026/27–2028/29
findings.detail: The Homelessness General Fund shows an unfavourable variance of £120,000, driven by budget needed to cover the Temporary Accommodation element of the Revenue Support Grant. This variance recurs across the three-year forecast period and is reported as a variance to be managed, suggesting it has not yet been funded.
findings.matters: Finance directors need to identify funding for unexpected homelessness pressures; peers in other councils watch whether this is sector-wide; lenders assess resilience to demand-led spending growth.
findings.figures: £120,000 variance in Homelessness General Fund line for 2026/27, 2027/28 and 2028/29

findings.paper_title: Enc. 2 for Budget Monitoring Report to 30 June 2026
findings.headline: Aquadrome Bridge Replacement forecast outturn increased by £260,000 to £281,975 following emergency decision on 25/2/26
findings.detail: Bridge remedial works required an emergency decision in February 2026. Originally budgeted at £21,975 (from 2025/26 rephasing), the forecast outturn is now £281,975. Spend to date at end of June was £169,007, indicating significant acceleration in works undertaken. This unplanned capital requirement accounts for the majority of the capital programme variance.
findings.matters: Unplanned capital requirements indicate asset condition or management issues that peers and lenders need to understand when assessing capital planning and financial stability
findings.figures: Budget increase £260,000; forecast outturn £281,975 against original phased budget £21,975; P3 spend £169,007
findings.quote: Increase in budget for remedial works to the bridge was agreed by urgent decision 25/2/26

findings.paper_title: Budget Outturn Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Original budget revised downward by £1.130m during the year due to inflation and cost pressures
findings.detail: The budget agreed in January 2025 was £1.130m higher than the revised budget used for outturn comparison. The revision occurred during the year to reflect cost pressures from persistent inflation, pay awards, and utilities costs.
findings.matters: Mid-year budget revisions of this scale indicate the council's budget planning underestimated cost pressures and had to be corrected in-year, suggesting either optimistic assumptions or forecasting weakness.
findings.figures: £1.130m budget reduction
findings.quote: The latest agreed budget was £1.130m lower than the original budget agreed in January 2025, after allowing for carry forwards from 2024/25. During the year the budget was amended to reflect cost pressures primarily arising from the impact of persistently high inflation. This cost pressure included the agreed pay award and increased supplier costs for utilities.

findings.paper_title: Budget Outturn Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Pay award for 2026/27 identified as most significant budget risk with negotiations expected to be protracted
findings.detail: The council has no settled pay award assumption for 2026/27 and expects negotiations to be protracted with the final position remaining unknown well into the financial year. Updates will follow in September budget monitoring.
findings.matters: Unbudgeted pay costs will force service cuts or further use of reserves. Pay is the largest controllable cost in local government and uncertainty creates real budget risk.
findings.figures: No financial impact quantified yet; update due September 2026
findings.quote: The most significant risk to the budget is the pay award for 2026/27. An update on the estimated financial impact in 2026/27 will be included in the Budget Monitoring report in September. It is likely that the pay negotiations will be protracted, and the final position will remain unknown well into the financial year.

findings.paper_title: Budget Outturn Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Capital programme slippage of £10.995m on Local Authority Housing Fund properties pushed to 2026/27
findings.detail: The council is rephasing £10.995m of capital budget for LAHF housing delivery (garage site development and property purchases) into 2026/27, representing 74% of the total £14.831m capital programme rephasing. The reasons for delay are not detailed.
findings.matters: Major capital delivery delays suggest project management challenges or implementation constraints and could affect the council's ability to deliver housing commitments and housing fund deadlines.
findings.figures: £10.995m rephasing against total capital rephasing of £14.831m
findings.quote: The most significant variation relates to the budget related to the delivery of Local Authority Housing Fund (LAHF) properties. Rephasing of £10.995m into 2026/27 is required in order to deliver the new housing as part of the LAHF delivery of the garage sites and purchase of additional properties.

findings.paper_title: Budget Outturn Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Disclaimed audit opinions in prior years have triggered increased external audit fees and remediation work
findings.detail: The council incurred higher external audit costs during 2025/26 due to 'build back work required as a result of disclaimed audit opinions in prior years.' Disclaimed audit opinions indicate the auditors could not form an opinion on the financial statements, signalling prior governance or accounting issues that required remediation.
findings.matters: Disclaimed opinions and post-audit remediation work indicate governance or financial reporting issues. A lender needs confidence in the reliability of a council's financial reporting and the quality of its controls.
findings.figures: Increased audit fees mentioned but amount not separately quantified in the outturn
findings.quote: A variance on Corporate Management Costs as a result of increased external audit fees arising from the build back work required as a result of disclaimed audit opinions in prior years.

findings.paper_title: Annual Governance Statement 2025/26
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation to unitary status in April 2028 creates staffing, service continuity and financial commitment risks
findings.detail: Hertfordshire is moving to unitary government in April 2028. This is identified as a significant governance issue bringing 'additional risks around staffing and day to day service operation in the period leading to and post reorganisation' and requiring 'additional consideration of long term commitments, contract and partnership arrangements'. The council is managing through communication, succession planning and partnership working, but the outcome is uncertain.
findings.matters: Local government reorganisations are high-risk periods with track records of service disruption, staff turnover, and unexpected financial pressures. A council preparing for absorption into a larger unit in two years faces uncertainty over future budget settlement, service scope, and officer roles. Lenders need confidence that the council can maintain financial stability through this transition.
findings.figures: April 2028 is the target date for reorganisation
findings.quote: Hertfordshire is currently expected to be part of the currently proposed round of Local Government Reorganisation to move to unitary government from April 2028. This will bring additional risks around staffing and day to day service operation in the period leading to and post reorganisation and require additional consideration of long term commitments, contract and partnership arrangements.

findings.paper_title: Annual Governance Statement 2025/26
findings.headline: Business rates revaluation creates significant appeal risk centred on a single major valuation (Warner Brothers)
findings.detail: Three Rivers had the highest increase in business rates from the national revaluation, largely driven by a single large valuation. The council faces significant appeal risk on this valuation which could impact the MTFS if the appeal succeeds. The council is managing the risk through the Collection Fund Reserve, which it describes as 'strong', but a successful appeal would erode income assumed in budget plans.
findings.matters: A successful business rates appeal by a major ratepayer could reduce income assumed in the MTFS. For a small district council, revenue dependency on few large businesses is a concentration risk. The reserve may not be sufficient if appeals are large.
findings.figures: Three Rivers had the highest increase in business rates following national revaluation; primary driver is Warner Brothers valuation
findings.quote: Three Rivers had the highest increase in business rates as a result of the national revaluation exercise. This was largely due to the increase in Warners Brothers valuation. This gives the Council a significant business rate appeal risk which could impact on the MTFS.

findings.paper_title: Annual Governance Statement 2025/26
findings.headline: Disclaimed audit opinions on prior year accounts (2020/21-2024/25) signal persistent accounting control problems
findings.detail: The council received disclaimed audit opinions on 2020/21, 2021/22, 2022/23 accounts under statutory backstop dates, and again on 2024/25 because of a buildup requiring accounts to be reaudited. Azets (the external auditor since 2023/24) could not provide assurance that the accounts fairly present the council's position. Recovery is uncertain and depends on whether 2025/26 audit can rebuild confidence.
findings.matters: Disclaimed opinions mean auditors cannot verify financial statements. A lender needs confidence in account integrity to assess financial position. Multiple years of disclaimed opinions suggest material weaknesses in systems or controls that have not yet been resolved.
findings.figures: 2020/21, 2021/22, 2022/23, 2024/25 all disclaimed; statutory backstop 13 December 2024 for 2022/23; 2025/26 backstop 31 January 2027
findings.quote: assurance could not be provided due to disclaimed prior year audits and therefore a disclaimed audit opinion was issued for the 2024/25 accounts. Due to a build back of the accounts being required by audit a disclaimed opinion was given for 2024/25. Officers will work with external audit to rebuild assurance through the 2025/26 audit onwards.

findings.paper_title: Financial planning - Revenue
findings.headline: Pay award inflation risk acknowledged; any increase above 3% must be absorbed from existing budgets with no growth room
findings.detail: The council budgets for 3% pay awards, but flags risk of higher awards given cost-of-living pressures above Bank of England targets. Critically: 'any increase will need to be balanced against affordability' and 'must be funded from existing budgets' – indicating zero flexibility to absorb pay inflation without service cuts or reserve drawdown.
findings.matters: Pay typically exceeds 40% of council budgets. Unbudgeted pay inflation with zero headroom forces either service reductions or reserve drawdown, both damaging to financial resilience.
findings.figures: Pay award assumption: 3% in 2026/27 and future years; any increase must be funded from existing budgets
findings.quote: There is a risk that the pay award could be higher as the increase to cost of living is above the BoE target. However, any increase will need to balanced against affordability for the sector, and Government public sector austerity targets, as any pay award will need to be funded from existing budgets.

findings.paper_title: Financial planning - Revenue
findings.headline: General Fund balance forecast to decline from £4.5m to £4.2m over medium term, supported by recurring small deficits
findings.detail: The council forecasts modest deficits in 2026/27 (£92k), 2027/28 (£110k), and 2028/29 (£155k) to be covered from reserves. This creates a declining reserve trajectory while the council simultaneously acknowledges that 'long term use of reserves to offset deficits is not sustainable or prudent'.
findings.matters: Declining reserves with structural deficits indicate the council's underlying revenue does not cover base costs. Sustainability depends on no cost shocks or income volatility beyond forecast.
findings.figures: General Fund balance: £4,546k (2025/26) declining to £4,189k (2028/29); minimum required £2,000k; balance declining as multiple of minimum
findings.quote: The long term use of reserves to offset deficits is not sustainable or prudent. However, the forecast indicates that general balances will remain well above the risk assessed level of £2.000m over the MTFP period

findings.paper_title: Financial planning - Revenue
findings.headline: £1 million reserve committed to local government reorganisation transition, occurring while council forecasts structural deficits
findings.detail: Three Rivers has ringfenced £1m from the Collection Fund Reserve for transition costs to the new unitary authority planned for 2028/29. This is a fixed cost commitment occurring at a time when the council is already forecasting small annual deficits.
findings.matters: The reorganisation is a known drain on reserves occurring when the council's underlying budget position shows ongoing deficits; it reduces headroom for unexpected cost pressures during transition.
findings.figures: £1m transfer to Local Government Reform Reserve; total reserves forecast to decline from £5.6m (2025/26) to £5.2m (2028/29)
findings.quote: £1m will be transferred from the Collection Fund reserve to the Local Government Reform reserve to provide resources for transition to the new Unitary authorities.

findings.paper_title: Financial planning - Revenue
findings.headline: Government funding system changes create volatility that council is hedging with reserve drawdown rather than forecasting with confidence
findings.detail: The Fair Funding Review and Business Rates Reset for 2026/27 introduce significant system changes with a higher business rates tariff for Three Rivers. The council explicitly states it is using the Collection Fund Reserve to 'balance' government income volatility. Commentators expect 'more challenge than would usually be the case' to the provisional settlement.
findings.matters: Using reserves to hedge government funding uncertainty reduces financial resilience. The council is consuming the reserve buffer that should cover cost shocks or income shortfalls.
findings.figures: Business Rates/RSG forecast: £3.0m (2025/26), £3.5m (2026/27), £4.0m (2027/28-2028/29); provisional settlement only, final due January 2026
findings.quote: Given the level of the risk around the numbers in the provisional settlement, business rate and revenue support grant income have been balanced against the Collection Fund Reserve which is used to manage the fluctuations in business rates that occur due to the way the system is implemented.

findings.paper_title: Financial planning - Revenue
findings.headline: Council tax base growth slowed in 2025/26, creating a £254k deficit recovery requirement in 2026/27
findings.detail: Tax base growth underperformed forecast, generating a Collection Fund deficit of £254k that must be recovered from council revenue in 2026/27. Since each 1% of tax base growth generates approximately £85k, this represents growth of ~3% below expectation.
findings.matters: Tax base shortfalls signal weaker property growth or collection weakness and directly reduce available revenue. Unlike discretionary savings, this cannot be offset by service cuts.
findings.figures: £0.254m Collection Fund deficit; Council Tax base increase 0.21% in 2026/27
findings.quote: For 2026/27, a deficit of £0.254m in relation to Council Tax will be recovered from Three Rivers as a result of slower than forecast tax base growth in 2025/26.

findings.paper_title: Three Rivers DC - Audit Completion Report - 2024.25 - FINAL
findings.headline: Adjustments to financial statements totalling £310k improvement to outturn
findings.detail: The auditor identified six adjustments to the financial statements that resulted in a net £310k improvement to reported financial outturn. Management has agreed to amend the accounts for all adjustments identified.
findings.matters: Material adjustments to the outturn position indicate the originally reported position was misstated. While this is an improvement, it raises questions about the quality of management's initial reporting.
findings.figures: Six adjustments totalling £310k improvement; four disclosure amendments also required
findings.quote: From the work we have completed, we have identified 6 adjustments to the financial statements that have resulted in a £310k improvement to your reported financial outturn.

findings.paper_title: Three Rivers DC - Audit Completion Report - 2024.25 - FINAL
findings.headline: Four-year build-back plan required to recover assurance over disclaimed audit years
findings.detail: Recovery of audit assurance from the four disclaimed years (2020/21-2023/24) is planned to take until 2027/28. This involves comprehensive risk assessment, substantive procedures on Property, Plant & Equipment, and the income strip scheme across multiple years. The complexity is compounded by the council's group accounts structure and income strip arrangements.
findings.matters: Multi-year recovery processes indicate fundamental issues with the prior audit trail. Lenders face ongoing uncertainty until all prior years are recovered, and the council will be subject to heightened audit scrutiny and costs for the next three years.
findings.figures: Indicative build-back plan from 2024/25 to 2027/28; four consecutive prior years disclaimed
findings.quote: It is important to note that build back is a comprehensive and time-consuming process which is compounded at a council such as Three Rivers where added complexity is present by virtue of the group accounts, income strip arrangement and other complexities within the asset portfolio.

findings.paper_title: Three Rivers DC - Audit Completion Report - 2024.25 - FINAL
findings.headline: Significant weaknesses in draft accounts quality and preparation controls
findings.detail: The Council reissued its draft financial statements on 29 September 2025, three months after the statutory 30 June deadline. The auditor identified a high number of errors including material errors, formula errors, and inconsistencies. Material changes were made to prior-year comparators in the reissued version, including changes to MRP charged and General Fund balance that should not have been amended.
findings.matters: Weaknesses in financial reporting controls and the late restatement of prior-year figures indicate issues with financial management governance and the reliability of the accounts preparation process.
findings.figures: Reissued 29 September 2025 (90 days late); material changes to prior-year comparators including MRP and closing General Fund balance
findings.quote: The Council issued its 2024/25 draft financial statements by the statutory reporting date of 30 June 2025. However, the Council subsequently amended and revised these statements and re-issued them on 29 September 2025... This level of error indicates weaknesses in the Council's quality assurance processes over the preparation of the draft accounts.

findings.paper_title: Three Rivers DC - Audit Completion Report - 2024.25 - FINAL
findings.headline: Wimbledon income strip asset understated by £400k in prior years; £3.5m sinking fund treatment still unresolved
findings.detail: The leased asset in the complex Wimbledon income strip scheme was undervalued in 2022/23; management challenged the valuer and obtained a new valuation, resulting in a restatement. A sinking fund contribution of £3.5 million received to cover tenant payment risks and refurbishment has been included in the restated asset and liability values. The auditor has not yet concluded whether this treatment is appropriate.
findings.matters: The income strip is financially significant and affects multiple financial statement line items. Material valuation errors and unresolved accounting treatment on a £3.5m contingency could mask the true economic position of a major asset.
findings.figures: Prior period adjustment understated by £400k; sinking fund contribution £3.5 million
findings.quote: we have identified that the prior period adjustment in the asset valuation was understated by £400k... A sinking fund contribution of £3.5 million paid to the Council to cover for risks associated with non-payment of tenants and any refurbishment has been received in 2022/23 has been included in the restated right-of-use asset and lease liability. We are considering the appropriateness of this treatment as part of our work.

findings.paper_title: Three Rivers DC - Audit Completion Report - 2024.25 - FINAL
findings.headline: Auditors intend to disclaim the opinion on 2024/25 financial statements
findings.detail: The auditor cannot form an opinion on Three Rivers' 2024/25 accounts and will disclaim, making it five consecutive years without an audit opinion. This is driven by the statutory backstop deadline of 27 February 2026 preventing completion of all necessary procedures. The lack of assurance on opening balances from prior disclaimed years means the auditor cannot gain sufficient evidence on the material accuracy of balances at 31 March 2025.
findings.matters: A disclaimed opinion means financial statements have not been verified by an independent auditor. For lenders assessing creditworthiness, this removes a critical control and creates uncertainty about the reliability of reported financial position.
findings.figures: Five consecutive years (2020/21-2024/25) without an unmodified audit opinion; backstop deadline 27 February 2026
findings.quote: Due to the challenges of undertaking an audit where the previous four years have been disclaimed because of the local authority backstop, it has not been possible to regain full assurance, and it is not possible for us to undertake sufficient work to support an unmodified audit opinion ahead of the backstop date of 27 February 2026.

findings.paper_title: Financial Planning - Capital Strategy and the Treasury Management Policy
findings.headline: Commercial income now 7.5% of net revenue in 2026/27, with exposure concentrated in property and joint venture returns
findings.detail: Net income from commercial investments reaches £1.083m in 2026/27 against a net revenue stream of £14.531m (7.5% ratio). This income is volatile by nature and exposes the council's core service funding to property market downturns and joint venture underperformance.
findings.matters: High exposure to commercial income creates revenue risk if the council cannot absorb losses; this flows through to ability to service debt
findings.figures: Commercial Investment Income 2026/27: £1.083m; Net Revenue Stream: £14.531m; Ratio: 7.5%
findings.quote: Net income from commercial investments comprises net income from financial investments (other than treasury management investments), together with net income from other assets held primarily for financial return, such as commercial property.

findings.paper_title: Financial Planning - Capital Strategy and the Treasury Management Policy
findings.headline: Council's risk appetite increasing as it expands into commercial property and major investments
findings.detail: The paper states: 'The Council's risk appetite is evolving as it becomes involved in a wider range of major property lead investments both within its economic area linked to regeneration and more widely for income generation purposes.' This signals a deliberate shift toward higher-risk income generation strategies.
findings.matters: Lenders monitor councils moving from core service funding to commercial investment models; increased risk appetite can signal future stress if income streams underperform
findings.figures: Commercial investment income 7.5% of net revenue stream in 2026/27, rising from 6.2% in 2024/25
findings.quote: The Council's risk appetite is evolving as it becomes involved in a wider range of major property lead investments both within its economic area linked to regeneration and more widely for income generation purposes.

findings.paper_title: Financial Planning - Capital Strategy and the Treasury Management Policy
findings.headline: Borrowing £16.4m in 2025/26 for housing projects with debt service dependent on external housing company repayments
findings.detail: The council has borrowed £16.393m predominantly for Local Authority Housing Fund projects through Three Rivers Homes Ltd. Crucially, 'Borrowing in 2025/26 arises predominantly as a result of the major projects and will be repaid in line with repayments made by Watford Community Housing and Three Rivers Homes Ltd.' If these external entities underperform, the council must absorb MRP and interest costs from its own budget.
findings.matters: Lenders need to assess whether the council can service debt if joint venture partners fail to generate expected repayments
findings.figures: £17.174m major projects funding; £16.393m borrowing in 2025/26; subsequent years £2.550m+ borrowing
findings.quote: Borrowing in 2025/26 arises predominantly as a result of the major projects and will be repaid in line with repayments made by Watford Community Housing and Three Rivers Homes Ltd.

findings.paper_title: Financial Planning - Capital Strategy and the Treasury Management Policy
findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement growing significantly and subject to audit restatement
findings.detail: The council's CFR (underlying borrowing need) is rising from £71.554m to £92.340m over the planning period. However, the paper notes: 'the opening CFR is subject to restatement following the conclusion of the outstanding external audits.' This means the baseline for assessing debt sustainability is not yet confirmed.
findings.matters: Lenders and finance directors need certainty on actual debt levels before assessing sustainability; an upward restatement could worsen affordability metrics
findings.figures: Opening CFR £71.554m (2025/26), Closing CFR £92.340m (2028/29)
findings.quote: Note the opening CFR is subject to restatement following the conclusion of the outstanding external audits.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1- Treasury Management - Mid-Year Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Liability benchmark deteriorates from £25.6m resource surplus to £0.2m by March 2028, signalling imminent borrowing pressure.
findings.detail: Forecast net loans requirement moves from (£25.600m) at March 2025 through (£7.600m) and (£3.800m) to (£0.200m) by March 2028. This dramatic erosion of the resource buffer means balance sheet resources will be depleted within three years, forcing external borrowing to fund capital plans.
findings.matters: Forecast signals the council will exhaust its financial cushion and need to access capital markets within three years, with limited flexibility for unexpected pressures or changed circumstances.
findings.quote: Whilst borrowing may be above the liability benchmark, strategies involving borrowing which is significantly above the liability benchmark carry higher risk.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1- Treasury Management - Mid-Year Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Borrowing Capital Financing Requirement forecast to grow 78% in one year, from £20.578m to £36.507m.
findings.detail: The council plans capital expenditure of £2.7m annually, driving the borrowing CFR from £20.578m to £36.507m by March 2026. Overall CFR grows from £66.943m to £82.872m. This substantial capital expansion creates refinancing risk, particularly at a time when PWLB 10-year rates are at 5.53%.
findings.matters: Rapid expansion of capital financing requirements means the council will need to borrow significantly more, at elevated interest rates, raising long-term affordability and refinancing risks.
findings.figures: Total CFR: £66.943m to £82.872m; Borrowing CFR: £20.578m to £36.507m

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1- Treasury Management - Mid-Year Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Wimbledon Investment lease liability of £46.438m is a major fixed-cost obligation far exceeding external borrowing.
findings.detail: The council has £46.438m in lease liabilities related entirely to the Wimbledon Investment, taking total debt to £54.438m. This compares to only £8m in external borrowing, making the lease the council's primary debt burden. It represents a long-term fixed cost that must be serviced regardless of revenue performance.
findings.matters: Large lease liabilities reduce financial flexibility and create a structural cost burden that constrains the council's ability to respond to pressures or fund other priorities.
findings.figures: £46.438m lease liability; total debt £54.438m versus external borrowing £8.0m
findings.quote: Debt other than borrowing stood at £46.438m on 30th September 2025, taking total debt to £54.438m.  The lease liability of £46.438m relates entirely to the Wimbledon Investment.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1- Treasury Management - Mid-Year Report 2025-26
findings.headline: The liability benchmark forecast shows the council shifting from net investor to net borrower position within the current financial year
findings.detail: The liability benchmark prudential indicator measures whether the council is a long-term net investor or borrower. At 31 March 2025, the council shows a negative liability benchmark of -£15.6m, indicating net investor status. The forecast for 31 March 2026 (end of current year) shifts dramatically to +£2.4m, indicating the council will require external borrowing. This one-year transition signals rapidly tightening finances driven by capital expenditure plans funded against declining reserves.
findings.matters: The speed of this transition (within 12 months) and the magnitude of the shift (£18m movement) indicate financial stress is arriving faster than might be expected. The council will need to access markets at unfavorable rates at precisely the moment its financial flexibility is constrained
findings.figures: Liability benchmark -£15.6m (31.3.25 actual), +£2.4m (31.3.26 forecast), rising to +£9.8m (31.3.28); existing borrowing £8.0m throughout
findings.quote: The liability benchmark is an important tool to help establish whether the Council is likely to be a long-term borrower or long-term investor in the future, and so shape its strategic focus and decision making. It represents an estimate of the cumulative amount of external borrowing the Council must hold to fund its current capital and revenue plans while keeping treasury investments at the minimum level of £0.1m required to manage day-to-day cash flow.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1- Treasury Management - Mid-Year Report 2025-26
findings.headline: The council faces material interest rate shock: forecast external borrowing will cost 2-2.5x more than existing debt at current market rates
findings.detail: The council's existing PWLB borrowing carries interest at 2.41%. Current PWLB rates for 10-year loans are 5.38-5.53%, with 20-year rates at 5.71-6.30%. Rates have moved higher during the period amid inflation and government fiscal concerns. This represents a doubling or more of borrowing costs if new external financing is required.
findings.matters: If the council accesses capital markets in the current environment, debt service costs will increase dramatically, materially impacting revenue budget affordability. This risk intensifies if the council's reserve depletion forces external borrowing sooner than planned
findings.figures: Existing PWLB rate 2.41%; 10-year PWLB rates 5.38-5.53%; 20-year rates 5.71-6.30%; rate range during period 5.17%-6.30%
findings.quote: The PWLB certainty rate for 10-year maturity loans was 5.38% at the beginning of the period and 5.53% at the end. The lowest available 10-year maturity certainty rate was 5.17% and the highest was 5.62%. Rates for 20-year maturity loans ranged from 5.71% to 6.30% during the period

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1- Treasury Management - Mid-Year Report 2025-26
findings.headline: The Wimbledon Investment creates a £46.4m finance lease liability that represents 86% of the council's total debt
findings.detail: The council has financed a Wimbledon Investment through a finance lease arrangement. This lease liability of £46.4m stands as the dominant component of the council's total debt of £54.4m, with only £8m being PWLB borrowing. This creates a fixed, long-term obligation that must be serviced regardless of other financial circumstances and significantly constrains the council's debt capacity.
findings.matters: This material long-term liability is a first charge on the council's resources. Lenders must account for this existing commitment when assessing the council's capacity to service additional debt or manage financial shocks
findings.figures: £46.438m lease liability, £54.438m total debt, £8.000m PWLB borrowing
findings.quote: Debt other than borrowing stood at £46.438m on 30th September 2025, taking total debt to £54.438m. The lease liability of £46.438m relates entirely to the Wimbledon Investment.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Report
findings.headline: Finance lease accounting inflates Capital Financing Requirement by £45m with no underlying cash impact
findings.detail: The Council's reported Capital Financing Requirement of £80.9m includes £45.1m for a Wimbledon property lease. This is a pure accounting adjustment under IFRS16 reflecting annual revaluation for lease indexation. The Council explicitly confirms this adjustment 'does not increase the actual amount of cash payable by the authority,' meaning the headline CFR significantly overstates true borrowing need.
findings.matters: The true loans-based borrowing need is only £30.4m (£80.9m CFR minus £45.1m lease), not the reported £80.9m. Lenders assessing debt ratios and borrowing capacity need the underlying position. The £45m accounting adjustment substantially obscures the Council's actual financial condition.
findings.figures: Finance Lease CFR £45.122m; Total reported CFR £80.894m; Actual Loans CFR £30.372m
findings.quote: This recalculation increases the CFR related to the lease, but as an accounting adjustment it does not increase the actual amount of cash payable by the authority.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Report
findings.headline: Three Rivers assumes contingent joint liability for West Herts Crematorium's £6m borrowing
findings.detail: Following the consolidation of West Herts Crematorium, Three Rivers Council is now jointly liable for the crematorium's £6m borrowing in the event that the crematorium cannot meet its obligations. Joint Committee members, including Three Rivers, share this liability as a contingent debt that could crystallize if the crematorium's financial position deteriorates.
findings.matters: Contingent liabilities represent potential future borrowing obligations that may not appear in headline debt figures. A £6m contingent liability is material to a local authority and creates unquantified debt risk. Lenders must assess all potential obligations including those from partner entity failures.
findings.figures: £6.0m West Herts Crematorium borrowing subject to joint liability
findings.quote: Joint Committee members are liable for their share of the loan in the unlikely event that the crematorium cannot meet its obligations

news_drafts.headline: Three Rivers forecasts £0.4m day-to-day overspend for 2026/27 and a £1.23m draw on reserves
news_drafts.lead:
Three Rivers District Council expects to spend £16.376m on day-to-day running costs (revenue spending) in 2026/27, £0.400m more than its latest budget of £15.976m, according to the budget monitoring report to 30 June 2026 (the in-year check of spending against budget). Policy and Resources accounts for the largest share of the variance at £217,000, followed by General Public Services at £178,000 and Climate Change and Leisure at £5,000. Supplementary estimates, extra budget approvals, of £0.272m have been requested.

The council's forecast sets net spending of £16,376,491 against income of £15,146,087 from council tax, government grants and business rates. That leaves a deficit of £1,230,403, to be met from the general fund balance. Deficits of £593,418 in 2027/28 and £642,913 in 2028/29 are also forecast and are likewise funded from that balance. In the General Public Services and Community Engagement Committee, forecast spending is £6.721m against a budget of £6.543m, a variance of £178,000, or 2.7%, after three months.

Homelessness shows a £120,000 adverse variance, which the council attributes to higher temporary accommodation costs. It is being met from the temporary accommodation element of the Revenue Support Grant, alongside grants of £329,704 for homelessness and rough sleeping and £108,733 for the Renters' Rights Act. At Watersmeet, an inflationary rise in the cleaning contract puts the forecast at £70,218 against a budget of £64,938, a £5,280 variance that is forecast to repeat in each of the next two years.

news_drafts.headline: Three Rivers forecasts £0.4m day-to-day overspend for 2026/27, with £1.23m deficit met from reserves
news_drafts.lead:
Three Rivers District Council expects to spend £16.376m on day-to-day running costs this year against a budget of £15.976m, an overspend of £0.400m. The figure comes from the first in-year check of spending against budget (budget monitoring), covering the period to 30 June 2026, reported to the Policy and Resources Committee. All three service committees are forecasting overspends.

Policy and Resources accounts for £217k, 4.2% of its £5.193m budget. General Public Services accounts for £178k and Climate Change and Leisure for £5k. The papers attribute the overspend mainly to changes in shared services arrangements with Watford Borough Council, under which temporary accommodation now forms part of the Revenue Support Grant, and to inflation on contracts. Within Policy and Resources, ICT charges are up £67k and HR charges £44k, reflecting higher charges from Watford. The elections contract adds £28.4k and office services £10.7k. The council is managing £74.9k of the variance by releasing budgeted contributions to money set aside (reserves), leaving about £142k not yet explained.

The council had budgeted for a deficit of £830,457 this year. The forecast is now £1,230,403, to be met from its general reserve, the working balance for its services. That reserve is forecast to fall from £5.18m to £3.95m, against a suggested prudent minimum of £2m. Deficits of £593,418 in 2027/28 and £642,913 in 2028/29 would take it to £2.71m by the end of 2028/29.
